content: 1. Ketoprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, antimigraine, antirheumatic, and musculoskeletal agent properties. It is FDA-approved for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, pain, and dysmenorrhea. 2. WikiDoc provides educational content based on FDA package inserts, the National Library of Medicine, and clinical practice guidelines but does not replace professional healthcare providers or promote off-label medication use inconsistent with labeling. 3. Ketoprofen carries a Black Box Warning due to potential risks, including cardiovascular and gastrointestinal adverse events. 4. Common adverse reactions to ketoprofen include edema, rash, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, flatulence, indigestion, nausea, elevated liver function tests, central nervous system (CNS) depression or stimulation, dizziness, headache, abnormal vision, tinnitus, and renal impairment. 5. The FDA-recommended adult dosage for ketoprofen is 75 mg orally every 8 hours or 50 mg orally every 6 hours, with a maximum daily dose of 300 mg. Higher doses do not provide additional analgesic benefits. 6. Ketoprofen is contraindicated in patients with a history of asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions to aspirin or other NSAIDs, and it should not be used for perioperative pain in coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. 7. Cardiovascular risks associated with NSAIDs, including ketoprofen, include an increased risk of thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke. Patients with cardiovascular disease or risk factors should use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration. 8. NSAIDs, including ketoprofen, can cause serious gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events such as inflammation, bleeding, ulceration, and perforation, which may occur without warning. Patients with a history of GI ulcers or bleeding are at higher risk. 9. Renal toxicity, including renal papillary necrosis and renal injury, has been observed with long-term NSAID use. Patients with impaired renal function, heart failure, liver dysfunction, or those taking diuretics or ACE inhibitors are at greater risk. 10. Emergency care should be sought if such reactions occur. 11. Serious skin reactions, including exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported with ketoprofen. Patients should discontinue use at the first sign of skin rash or hypersensitivity. 12. 13. Adverse reactions observed in clinical trials include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, flatulence, anorexia, vomiting, stomatitis, headache, dizziness, somnolence, malaise, depression, insomnia, nervousness, tinnitus, visual disturbances, rash, and renal impairment. 14. Ketoprofen may interact with other drugs, including ACE inhibitors, diuretics, lithium, methotrexate, probenecid, and warfarin, potentially increasing the risk of adverse effects or toxicity. 15. In elderly patients, ketoprofen clearance is reduced, and they may be more sensitive to its gastrointestinal and renal effects. Dosage adjustments and careful monitoring are recommended. 16. Ketoprofen is not recommended for use in pediatric patients under 18 years of age, and its safety and efficacy in this population have not been established. 17. In cases of overdose, symptoms may include lethargy, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, respiratory depression, coma, or convulsions. Management involves supportive care, as there is no specific antidote. 18. Ketoprofen exerts its effects by inhibiting prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis, stabilizing lysosomal membranes, and exhibiting antibradykinin activity, although its precise mechanism of action is not fully understood.
